title: Baby Girl's Skull With a Single Eye in the Middle of Her Face Found Near Peru's Nazca Lines

content:
The DNA of a baby girl buried about 1,600 years ago in southern Peru confirms that she was born with cyclopia, an extremely rare malformation that leaves a single eye socket in the center of the face. The cause was an extra copy of chromosome 13, and her burial shows no treatment different from that given to other Nazca children.

Two infants shared a single ceramic urn, stacked one above the other. The lower one had a single central eye socket instead of two and lacked nasal bones. They were buried about 1,600 years ago at Jauranga, a site in the Palpa Valley of southern Peru, a few miles from where the famous Nazca Lines were drawn.

Now DNA shows why one of the two was like that. The study was published Nov. 9, 2026, in the journal PNAS.

The work was carried out by a Peruvian, German and U.S. team that includes archaeologist Elsa Tomasto-Cagigao of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru and Lars Fehren-Schmitz, an ancient-DNA specialist at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

The authors combine three lines of evidence: the skeleton, the genetic material and the burial context. They use that combination to separate what can be known—the child’s condition—from what cannot: how her family experienced it and what care she received.

A Nazca cemetery in the Palpa Valley

The Nazca culture flourished on the southern coast of Peru from roughly two centuries before the Christian era to the sixth or seventh century A.D. It is famous for the enormous drawings traced across the desert.

Palpa, about 25 miles north of the modern city of Nazca, is one of the best-studied areas. A Peruvian-German project directed by Markus Reindel of the German Archaeological Institute and Johny Isla has worked there since 1997 and has documented more than 650 settlements in the region’s valleys.

Jauranga was first occupied in Paracas times, the culture that preceded the Nazca. Later, in the upper layers of the site, archaeologists opened 31 tombs from the phase they call Nazca Medium, dated to A.D. 325–440. In Europe, this was the age of the Council of Nicaea and Constantine, and it reaches to shortly after the Suebi, Vandals and Alans entered Hispania.

Burial No. 25 contained the complete skeletons of two infants inside a ceramic vessel, with no other grave goods recorded. Urn burial was common: according to the study, it accounts for about a quarter of documented Nazca tombs in Palpa and was used mainly for children under six.

What cyclopia is and why almost no one survives it

Cyclopia is the most severe form of a brain-development failure called holoprosencephaly. Around the fourth or fifth week of pregnancy, the front of the embryo’s brain should split into two halves. In these cases, it does not.

The condition is very rare. The study estimates it occurs in about one in 100,000 births and notes that it is almost always fatal before birth or shortly afterward.

The skull of the Jauranga baby, whom researchers call JA13A, matches modern clinical descriptions. It was small, with a circumference of 18 centimeters—about 7 inches, or just over half the usual size for a full-term newborn. It had a single central eye socket, no nasal bones and no internal walls between the orbits. The upper jaw was undivided.

The base of the skull showed a single opening for the optic nerve. There were also a tall, pointed skull, two incomplete vertebrae and a narrowing of the left clavicle.

Only bone survives, so the skeleton demonstrates a single central socket but cannot reveal what it contained or what the soft tissue of the face looked like.

The myth of Polyphemus, the giant shepherd in the Odyssey whom Odysseus blinds, has served for decades as a popular reference for this malformation. Some have proposed that cases like this could have contributed to the cyclops legend.

It is one hypothesis among others, including one formulated in 1914 by paleontologist Othenio Abel. He suggested that fossil skulls of dwarf elephants on Mediterranean islands, with their large central nasal opening, could have been mistaken for those of one-eyed giants.

The chromosome that did not belong

To find the origin of the problem, the authors sequenced DNA extracted from a tibia bone. Human cells normally carry two copies of each of the 23 types of chromosomes, the packages that store genetic material.

In trisomy 13, also called Patau syndrome, there are three copies of chromosome 13. It is one of the main chromosomal causes of severe holoprosencephaly and, according to the authors, accounts for 17% to 39% of cases.

The analysis of JA13A showed an excess of reads from chromosome 13 using three independent statistical methods and two types of genetic data, compared with 250 ancient South American genomes. The copy-number estimate came out slightly above three, and a statistical model clearly supported trisomy.

When the researchers reviewed all the chromosomes, chromosome 13 was the only one that produced a signal compatible with an extra copy. The DNA also indicates that the baby was a girl.

A short life whose length is unknown

JA13A’s teeth point to an age of between two and four months outside the womb. The long bones, by contrast, are the size of a near-term fetus.

That discrepancy could indicate that she survived for a time after birth, which is unusual in cyclopia. But the authors raise the possibility cautiously: trisomy 13 and severe holoprosencephaly can alter the normal growth rate of teeth and bones, so neither measure provides a reliable age. Postnatal survival is plausible, they conclude, but cannot be established.

The other baby, JA13B, had no anomalies and was somewhat less developed. Both are girls, but mitochondrial DNA, which is inherited only through the mother, reveals that they did not have the same mother. Why they were buried together remains unanswered. Tomasto-Cagigao says they appear to have been placed there in a single act.

A burial like other children’s

The social side of the story is perhaps the most delicate. The authors stress that a bodily difference detected in a skeleton does not by itself reveal whether that person was considered disabled or whether they received care. Both concepts depend on the society in question.

What is known is the treatment in death. Other infant urns at Palpa are simple and contain no offerings, and JA13A’s fits that pattern. Fehren-Schmitz summarizes the idea by saying that the girl was neither “excluded” because of her condition nor treated as “special.”

The researchers conclude that infant funerary traditions were maintained despite her appearance, though that does not show whether her condition affected her social identity or the care she received in life.

The case echoes another recent find. In 2024, a team led by Adam Rohrlach of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology published in Nature Communications the screening of nearly 10,000 ancient genomes. They found six cases of Down syndrome and one of Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18), all in infants, at sites in Spain, Bulgaria, Finland and Greece. Those authors noted that they knew of no previous case of trisomy 13 or 18 identified in ancient remains.

The Jauranga authors themselves warn against extrapolating. In the Andes, there is very diverse evidence of how bodily difference was treated. Moche iconography from the north coast shows people with visible congenital features in prestige contexts. There are skeletal remains of individuals with severe impairments who survived thanks to the care of others.

Inca and colonial sources, written 1,000 years later, describe everything from inclusion in community life to specialized ritual roles, but also exclusion and discrimination. None of those examples belongs to Nazca society, and the authors insist they should not be used as direct analogies.

A paradox remains. DNA has made it possible to explain precisely a malformation that has fascinated people for centuries, and the archaeological context shows that this girl was incorporated into usual funerary practices. How her community saw her while she lived, who her mother was, why she shared an urn with another baby from another mother: none of those questions has an answer in the skeleton, and the authors admit that it probably never will.
